1. Project Overview
Project Name
ChannelForge — Fiber Liquidity Readiness Engine
One-Sentence Summary
ChannelForge is an open-source Fiber infrastructure layer that helps payment applications determine whether a specific payment can be successfully received, identify liquidity shortages, recommend the minimum intervention required, and verify when the destination becomes payment-ready.
Project Type
Developer Tool · Payment Infrastructure · Ecosystem Infrastructure
2. Team Profile
Core Member
Wilson Momanyi Okeyo
Role: Blockchain Developer / CKB & Fiber Ecosystem Builder
Experience:
blockchain application development
blockchain infrastructure
developer tooling
smart contract development
Web3 ecosystem development
technical education and developer-focused initiatives
open-source blockchain projects
ChannelForge will initially be developed as an individual-led open-source project. The resulting code, documentation, tests, and demonstration will be publicly available to developers building on CKB and Fiber.
3. Project Background
Problem
Fiber provides fast, multi-asset payments through off-chain payment channels and multi-hop routing.
However, the existence of a payment route does not necessarily mean that the destination has enough usable inbound liquidity to receive the required payment amount.
For example, a merchant may need to receive:
50,000 RGB++ USDT
The Fiber network may have:
Connected peers
Supported asset
Available payment routes
But the merchant may only have:
31,700 usable inbound liquidity
The payment may therefore be unable to complete even though the merchant is connected to the network and a route appears to exist.
This creates a gap between:
Finding a payment route
↓
Having enough usable liquidity
↓
Being ready to receive the payment
Developers building payment applications currently need to reason about several variables themselves, including:
channel state
asset support
inbound and outbound liquidity
route availability
payment amount
routing costs
liquidity constraints
possible rebalancing actions
This makes it difficult to build applications that can predict whether a payment will actually succeed before attempting it.
The problem is especially relevant for:
merchants
wallets
payment processors
RGB++ applications
stablecoin applications
Fiber service providers
automated payment systems
The missing abstraction is not another payment route.
It is payment liquidity readiness.
Ecosystem Relevance
As Fiber expands its multi-asset payment capabilities, applications need better ways to understand whether liquidity is available where a payment needs to arrive.
ChannelForge introduces a simple application-level question:
Can this destination receive
this exact payment right now?
If the answer is no, ChannelForge should provide:
How much liquidity is missing?
↓
What intervention could resolve the shortage?
↓
Is the destination ready after the intervention?
This turns liquidity from something developers discover through failed payments into something they can analyze proactively.
4. Solution
Overview
ChannelForge is a browser/API-accessible and open-source infrastructure layer that turns Fiber’s channel and routing state into a programmable liquidity-readiness engine.
The project does not attempt to replace Fiber’s existing payment, routing, channel, or liquidity mechanisms.
Instead, it provides the missing application-level layer between Fiber’s network primitives and payment applications.
The first version focuses on:
Observe
↓
Analyze
↓
Recommend
↓
Verify
The Spark milestone will focus on four core components:
Payment Liquidity Intent
Liquidity Readiness Engine
Liquidity Intervention Recommendation
Payment-Ready Verification
Deliverable 1: Payment Liquidity Intent
Final Form
A machine-readable interface through which an application can specify exactly what liquidity it requires.
Example:
Payment Liquidity Intent
Asset:
RGB++ USDT
Destination:
Merchant Node
Required Amount:
50,000
Payment Deadline:
10 minutes
Maximum Cost:
0.5%
Minimum Readiness:
95%
Purpose
Instead of simply asking whether a destination is connected, applications can describe a concrete payment requirement.
ChannelForge uses this requirement as the input for its liquidity analysis.
Core Parameters
The initial specification will support:
asset
destination
required amount
payment deadline
maximum acceptable cost
minimum readiness requirement
Deliverable 2: Fiber Liquidity Readiness Engine
Final Form
A Fiber-integrated engine that analyzes relevant channel and routing conditions and determines whether the requested payment is currently feasible.
Example:
PAYMENT LIQUIDITY ANALYSIS
Required:
50,000
Usable inbound liquidity:
31,700
Liquidity deficit:
18,300
Best available route:
3 hops
Estimated cost:
0.18%
Status:
NOT PAYMENT-READY
Purpose
The engine converts raw Fiber network information into an application-friendly readiness result.
Core Features
The engine will analyze:
channel state
asset availability
destination connectivity
usable inbound liquidity
potential payment routes
liquidity requirements
estimated payment cost
payment-readiness conditions
Deliverable 3: Liquidity Intervention Recommendation
Final Form
When sufficient liquidity is not available, ChannelForge will provide an actionable recommendation.
Example:
PAYMENT LIQUIDITY ANALYSIS
Required:
50,000
Available:
31,700
Deficit:
18,300
Recommended intervention:
Circular rebalance
Expected liquidity:
50,000+
Status:
INTERVENTION REQUIRED
The MVP will focus on recommendation rather than autonomous fund movement.
This makes the first version safer and more achievable within the grant period.
The system will explain what liquidity is missing and what Fiber-compatible action could potentially resolve the shortage.
Future versions could extend this into:
Observe
↓
Analyze
↓
Recommend
↓
Execute
↓
Verify
Deliverable 4: Payment-Ready Verification
Final Form
After liquidity conditions change, ChannelForge will evaluate the original Payment Liquidity Intent again.
Example:
PAYMENT READY ✓
Required:
50,000
Usable inbound liquidity:
52,400
Best route:
3 hops
Estimated cost:
0.18%
Status:
READY
Purpose
Liquidity conditions can change dynamically.
ChannelForge therefore needs to verify that an intervention has actually produced the required payment conditions instead of assuming that the problem has been solved.
Core Workflow
Payment Liquidity Intent
↓
Fiber Network Analysis
↓
Liquidity Deficit Detection
↓
Intervention Recommendation
↓
Liquidity State Changes
↓
Payment-Ready Verification
↓
Payment
5. Technical Approach
Technology Stack
Core Engine:
Rust / Fiber-compatible infrastructure
Fiber Integration:
Fiber network and channel interfaces
Developer Interface:
CLI and API interface
Testing:
Fiber test environment and simulated payment scenarios
Documentation:
Markdown-based developer documentation
Deployment:
Public GitHub repository and reproducible demonstration environment
Architecture Overview
Fiber Network
│
┌───────────┴───────────┐
│ │
Channels Routes
│ │
└───────────┬───────────┘
↓
ChannelForge
│
┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
│ │ │
↓ ↓ ↓
Liquidity Analysis Route Analysis Readiness Engine
│ │ │
└────────────────┼────────────────┘
↓
Intervention
Recommendation
│
↓
Payment Ready
Key Technical Challenges
1. Modeling Usable Inbound Liquidity
Challenge:
A channel’s total capacity does not necessarily represent the amount that can currently be used to receive a particular payment.
Solution:
ChannelForge will analyze the relevant Fiber channel state and determine the usable liquidity available toward the destination for the requested asset and payment amount.
2. Determining Payment Readiness
Challenge:
A route may exist while the available liquidity is insufficient for the actual payment.
Solution:
ChannelForge will evaluate the complete Payment Liquidity Intent against current liquidity and routing conditions.
The result will be a clear readiness state:
PAYMENT READY
or:
NOT PAYMENT-READY
together with the relevant reason.
3. Identifying the Liquidity Deficit
Challenge:
A generic payment failure does not tell an application how much liquidity is missing.
Solution:
ChannelForge will calculate the difference between:
Required liquidity
-
Usable liquidity
and expose the result to developers.
Example:
Required:
50,000
Usable:
31,700
Deficit:
18,300
4. Producing Actionable Recommendations
Challenge:
Identifying a shortage is useful, but developers also need to understand what could resolve it.
Solution:
The recommendation engine will evaluate available Fiber-native liquidity mechanisms and identify an appropriate intervention, such as circular rebalancing where applicable.
The MVP will recommend actions rather than automatically controlling user funds.
5. Verifying Liquidity Changes
Challenge:
Fiber liquidity is dynamic and can change after payments, rebalancing, or channel updates.
Solution:
ChannelForge will re-evaluate the original Payment Liquidity Intent after a liquidity intervention.
The system will only report:
PAYMENT READY
when the defined conditions are satisfied.
6. To-Do List
Week 1: Architecture Design
Tasks:
define ChannelForge architecture
define Payment Liquidity Intent
identify required Fiber network state
design liquidity analysis model
establish Fiber test environment
Milestone:
ChannelForge architecture and Payment Liquidity Intent specification completed.
Week 2: Fiber Integration
Tasks:
integrate Fiber network information
integrate channel state
implement asset identification
establish test scenarios
create initial network-state adapter
Milestone:
ChannelForge can retrieve and process the required Fiber network information.
Week 3: Liquidity Analysis Engine
Tasks:
implement usable inbound liquidity calculation
implement liquidity deficit calculation
implement route analysis
implement estimated cost analysis
create structured analysis output
Milestone:
Working Fiber liquidity analysis engine.
Week 4: Readiness and Recommendation Engine
Tasks:
implement Payment Liquidity Intent evaluation
implement payment-readiness status
implement intervention recommendation logic
add edge-case handling
build initial CLI/API interface
Milestone:
Working readiness and recommendation system.
Week 5: Verification and Testing
Tasks:
implement post-intervention verification
test RGB++ scenarios
create integration tests
test different liquidity conditions
test failed and insufficient-liquidity scenarios
improve reliability
Milestone:
Complete end-to-end liquidity-readiness workflow.
Week 6: Finalization
Tasks:
polish CLI/API
complete technical documentation
create developer examples
prepare public repository
produce end-to-end demonstration
complete final tests
publish MVP
Milestone:
Public ChannelForge MVP release.
7. Required Funding
Total Requested
$1,000 USD
Funding Breakdown
Category
Amount
Core liquidity engine development
$400
Fiber/RGB++ integration and testing
$200
CLI/API implementation
$150
Testnet and demonstration infrastructure
$100

$100
Testing and final deployment
$50
Total
$1,000
Justification
The funding supports a focused six-week MVP development cycle.
The project prioritizes:
Fiber-native infrastructure
payment liquidity analysis
RGB++ compatibility
measurable technical deliverables
developer usability
open-source ecosystem value
The project intentionally does not attempt to build a full liquidity marketplace or autonomous liquidity-management system within this grant.
The requested funding is therefore focused on delivering a working and reusable liquidity-readiness infrastructure primitive.
8. Deliverables + How to Verify
Deliverable 1
Payment Liquidity Intent
Format:
Open-source specification and implementation.
Acceptance Criteria:
Developers can define a payment requirement containing:
asset
destination
amount
deadline
cost constraints
Verification
Steps:
Open the ChannelForge CLI/API.
Create a Payment Liquidity Intent.
Specify an asset, destination, and required amount.
Submit the intent.
Expected Result:
ChannelForge accepts the intent and generates a liquidity analysis request.
Deliverable 2
Fiber Liquidity Readiness Engine
Format:
Open-source code repository.
Acceptance Criteria:
Users can:
analyze Fiber channel state
identify usable inbound liquidity
calculate liquidity deficits
analyze potential routes
determine payment readiness
Verification
Steps:
Start a Fiber test environment.
Create a payment scenario.
Submit a Payment Liquidity Intent.
Run the ChannelForge analysis.
Expected Result:
The system returns a structured result such as:
Required:
50,000
Usable inbound:
31,700
Liquidity deficit:
18,300
Status:
NOT PAYMENT-READY
Deliverable 3
Liquidity Intervention Recommendation
Format:
Integrated software module.
Acceptance Criteria:
When insufficient liquidity is detected, ChannelForge produces an actionable recommendation.
Verification
Steps:
Create a payment intent requiring more liquidity than currently available.
Run liquidity analysis.
Review the recommendation.
Expected Result:
The system returns:
Liquidity deficit:
18,300
Recommended intervention:
Circular rebalance
Deliverable 4
Payment-Ready Verification
Format:
Integrated verification module.
Acceptance Criteria:
ChannelForge can determine whether the original payment intent becomes satisfiable after liquidity conditions change.
Verification

Apply the recommended liquidity intervention in the test environment.

Expected Result:
Required:
50,000
Usable inbound:
52,400
Status:
PAYMENT READY

Documentation and Demonstration

The final report will include:
repository link
demonstration link
architecture documentation
API/CLI documentation
screenshots

end-to-end demonstration
RGB++ test scenarios
development summary

problem analysis
Fiber ecosystem research
architecture planning
liquidity-readiness model

MVP scope definition
The project is currently at the design and architecture stage.

Build:
Fiber integration
liquidity analysis engine
Payment Liquidity Intent implementation
payment-readiness engine
liquidity deficit calculation
intervention recommendation system
payment-ready verification
CLI/API interface
automated tests
documentation
public demonstration
The funding will move ChannelForge from a defined architecture and concept into a working open-source MVP.
**
10. CKB Alignment**
ChannelForge directly supports the CKB ecosystem by improving the reliability and developer usability of Fiber-based payments.
The project focuses on the intersection of:
CKB assets
RGB++
Fiber payment channels
multi-hop routing
inbound liquidity
merchant payments
payment infrastructure
developer tooling
The initial implementation will use RGB++ assets as the primary use case, while keeping the underlying architecture sufficiently asset-generic to support other CKB/Fiber assets.
The ecosystem flow is:
CKB / RGB++
↓
Fiber
↓
Payment Channels
↓
Liquidity Analysis
↓
Payment Readiness
↓
Reliable Payment Applications
ChannelForge does not attempt to replace Fiber’s core payment-channel or routing infrastructure.
Instead, it provides a complementary developer infrastructure layer that helps applications understand one of the most important practical constraints of channel-based payments:
Is there enough usable liquidity at the destination for this payment?
This gives CKB/Fiber developers a higher-level primitive for building:
merchant payment systems
wallets
payment processors
RGB++ applications
stablecoin payment applications
Fiber service infrastructure
automated payment applications
The project also provides a natural foundation for future improvements in Fiber liquidity management.
The long-term vision is to make payment liquidity readiness a reusable primitive across the CKB payment ecosystem.
Instead of applications discovering liquidity problems only after a payment fails, they can proactively determine:
Can this destination receive this payment?
↓
How much liquidity is available?
↓
How much is missing?
↓
What intervention is required?
↓
Is the destination now ready?
Ultimately:
Fiber provides the payment network.
ChannelForge provides the liquidity intelligence that helps applications know when that network is ready for their payment.

  • Payment Liquidity Intent concept

  • MVP scope definition

The project is currently at the design and architecture stage.

Funded Work

During the Eco Fund development period:

Build:

  • Fiber integration

  • liquidity analysis engine

  • Payment Liquidity Intent implementation

  • payment-readiness engine

  • liquidity deficit calculation

  • intervention recommendation system

  • payment-ready verification

  • CLI/API interface

  • automated tests

  • documentation

  • public demonstration

The funding will move ChannelForge from a defined architecture and concept into a working open-source MVP.

**
10. CKB Alignment**

ChannelForge directly supports the CKB ecosystem by improving the reliability and developer usability of Fiber-based payments.

The project focuses on the intersection of:

  • CKB assets

  • RGB++

  • Fiber payment channels

  • multi-hop routing

  • inbound liquidity

  • merchant payments

  • payment infrastructure

  • developer tooling

The initial implementation will use RGB++ assets as the primary use case, while keeping the underlying architecture sufficiently asset-generic to support other CKB/Fiber assets.

The ecosystem flow is:

CKB / RGB++
      ↓
Fiber
      ↓
Payment Channels
      ↓
Liquidity Analysis
      ↓
Payment Readiness
      ↓
Reliable Payment Applications

ChannelForge does not attempt to replace Fiber’s core payment-channel or routing infrastructure.

Instead, it provides a complementary developer infrastructure layer that helps applications understand one of the most important practical constraints of channel-based payments:

Is there enough usable liquidity at the destination for this payment?

This gives CKB/Fiber developers a higher-level primitive for building:

  • merchant payment systems

  • wallets

  • payment processors

  • RGB++ applications

  • stablecoin payment applications

  • Fiber service infrastructure

  • automated payment applications

The project also provides a natural foundation for future improvements in Fiber liquidity management.

The long-term vision is to make payment liquidity readiness a reusable primitive across the CKB payment ecosystem.

Instead of applications discovering liquidity problems only after a payment fails, they can proactively determine:

Can this destination receive this payment?

        ↓

How much liquidity is available?

        ↓

How much is missing?

        ↓

What intervention is required?

        ↓

Is the destination now ready?

Ultimately:

Fiber provides the payment network.

ChannelForge provides the liquidity intelligence that helps applications know when that network is ready for their payment.

topics.title: CellScript - A DSL for Cell-Based Contracts

recent_posts.topic_title: CellScript - A DSL for Cell-Based Contracts
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
CellScript 0.25: More Expressive Contracts, Safer Upgrades, Stronger Verification
Short Announcement
CellScript 0.25 is out.
For contract authors, this release adds bounded non-Cell generics, Option<T>,
generic fixed arrays, full-range u128 literals, checked division and
remainder, bitwise and shift operators, recursive patterns, field-path borrows,
and labeled loop control.
For package maintainers, explicit public, public(package), and private
visibility now feeds a canonical package interface. cellc interface-diff
checks upgrades across source API, serialized layout, runtime ABI, effects,
builders, and deployment contracts.
For auditors, metadata schema 61 adds canonical typed semantics, and the
independent artifact checker binds that record through lowering to the final
RISC-V ELF with new V2419 and V2420 checks.
0.25 also fixes an unsafe bounded-collection lowering gap. Unsupported
consume_each and create_each paths now fail closed instead of compiling to
a false success. Positive runtime support remains deliberately deferred until
its consensus rules and adversarial CKB-VM evidence are complete.
For Contract Authors: More Reuse, Same Explicit Cell Ownership
Bounded generics for ordinary values
CellScript can now specialize generic value structs, enums, and pure functions
before IR lowering:
struct Pair<T: copy + drop + store + fixed + serializable + non_linear>
has copy, drop, store, fixed, serializable, non_linear
{
left: T,
right: T,
}
fn first<T: copy + drop + store + fixed + serializable + non_linear>(
pair: Pair<T>,
) -> T {
pair.left
}
The same checked path supports imported public templates. A package can use an
alias for a dependency and specialize its generic types or functions while the
specialization remains owned by the module that declared the template.
The boundary is intentionally narrow:
generic instantiation is deterministic and budgeted;
value abilities and phantom parameters are explicit;
abilities such as copy, drop, and store do not grant Cell lifecycle
authority;
ordinary generic containers cannot hide a resource, shared, or other
Cell-backed value.
This gives users reusable value code without introducing an object runtime or
weakening CellScript’s linear ownership model.
Useful built-ins and complete fixed-width operations
0.25 adds or completes:
built-in Option<T> using the checked fixed-width generic enum path;
generic fixed arrays;
decimal u128 literals across the full u128 range;
checked u128 division and remainder;
integer &, |, ^, <<, and >> lowering;
exact scalar and wide division-by-zero guards.
Wide operands now use a shared stack-spilled loading path, so resolving a
dynamic Molecule field cannot overwrite a live u128 limb. Constant folding
also refuses arithmetic that would wrap even though the runtime operation
would trap. Dynamic-schema CKB-VM vectors cover u128 addition, bitwise
operations, and shifts.
Patterns that work beyond the simplest case
match now supports recursive enum, tuple, and struct patterns, plus
binding-free or-patterns. Fixed tuple and array values can be materialized and
projected through the paths needed by nested payload matches.
Exhaustiveness checking uses a bounded constructor-matrix computation. Nested
and or-pattern coverage is merged instead of being approximated from the top
level, making useful matches accepted and incomplete ones rejected before
code generation.
Clearer borrowing and loop control
Read-only Cell views can borrow a field path and reborrow from the canonical
root. The compiler still rejects escaping the view, crossing a consume or
destroy operation, or using the borrow as persistent storage.
Loops now support break, continue, and label name: for/while. Valid
targets lower to explicit control-flow graph edges; an unknown or invalid
target is a compile-time error.
For Package Maintainers: Know What An Upgrade Changes
Top-level declarations can now be marked:
public
public(package)
private
Every successful compile emits a canonical
cellscript-package-interface-v2 record and interface_hash. Edition 2026
remains source compatible. If a module mixes explicit and implicit visibility,
the compiler emits W2500 instead of silently changing the default.
Generate an interface with:
cellc interface path/to/package --output target/package.interface.json
Compare two versions with:
cellc interface-diff \
--old target/old.interface.json \
--new target/new.interface.json
The report separates six kinds of compatibility:
source API;
serialized layout;
runtime ABI;
effects and capabilities;
generated builders;
deployment contracts.
A breaking report exits with stable diagnostic E2501. Additive exports still
change the interface hash, but they are reported as compatible.
Concrete monomorphizations are implementation evidence, not public exports.
Changing a private generic use site therefore does not create a public API
break. Registry publication signs and stores the canonical interface, the API
recomputes its hash and checks upgrade compatibility at admission, and the
standalone Registry verifier checks the stored binding again.
For Auditors: Follow Typed Intent To The Machine Artifact
0.24 introduced an independently checked four-file artifact bundle:
contract.elf
contract.elf.meta.json
contract.elf.lowering.json
contract.elf.sourcemap.json
0.25 moves that boundary closer to the programmer’s intent. Metadata schema 61
adds cellscript-typed-semantics-v2, covering:
canonical types and layouts;
locals and operations;
control-flow blocks and calls;
effects and ownership;
borrow regions;
owner-qualified generic instantiations.
Verified lowering record v3 accounts for each typed block and binds its
materialized hash to the entry ABI and final machine blocks. In plain language,
the evidence chain is:
typed program -> lowering blocks -> entry ABI -> final RISC-V machine ranges
The standalone cellscript-artifact-checker verifies that chain without
loading the parser, resolver, type checker, IR, optimizer, assembler, or code
generator. Its new stable rejection classes are:
V2419: malformed or inconsistent typed semantics;
V2420: a broken typed-record, lowering, ABI, or machine binding.
Deterministic mutation tests cover both classes. This makes compiler drift and
artifact tampering easier to detect independently.
The claim remains precise: this is bounded structural and typed verification.
It is not a general proof of source-to-machine semantic equivalence, CKB-VM
execution, deployment, commitment, or mainnet acceptance.
One Registry For Every Executable Surface
0.25 adds a compiler-owned registry of the IR and runtime surfaces that can
reach an executable artifact. It generates both Markdown and JSON support
matrices and is exhaustively matched by the compiler.
That changes failure behavior in two important ways:
a known but incomplete executable shape is rejected in strict production
compilation with E2105 before ASM or ELF is written;
a new IR variant or runtime feature cannot silently bypass the registry—it
must be classified or compilation fails.
Fail-closed runtime helpers remain defense in depth. They are no longer used to
make an unsupported feature look production-ready.
An Important Safety Fix For Bounded Collections
During the 0.25 audit, we found a serious gap in consume_each and
create_each.
The frontend and ownership checker accepted the bounded operation, but IR
lowering replaced its body with Unit. That meant a body containing
require false could compile into an action that returned success without
scanning, checking, consuming, or creating anything.
0.25 removes that path:
typed IR retains the predicate or create template;
lowering inserts an explicit registered fail-closed call;
permissive artifacts return stable runtime error 24,
collection-runtime-unsupported, in CKB-VM;
--production and --deny-fail-closed stop with E2105 before producing
ASM or ELF;
the diagnostic names the operation, source location, missing ProofPlan tier,
and a concrete remediation;
entry ABI and ProofPlan metadata no longer claim supported pointers or
runtime-observed cardinality when no runtime scan exists.
This is a safety fix, not positive runtime support for bounded lifecycle
collections. The remaining work needs exact transaction-group selection,
canonical Cell and witness decoding, output order and one-to-one
correspondence, identity rules, capacity rules, and positive and adversarial
CKB-VM vectors. 0.25 does not invent those consensus semantics.
For Playground And VS Code Users
The browser Playground now understands the 0.25 authoring surface:
generics, abilities, and visibility;
bitwise and shift operators;
recursive patterns;
field-path borrows;
labeled loop control.
The compiler returns a bounded authoring summary for the Cell Flow, action,
type, and raw-metadata panels. Full public-interface, typed-semantics,
ProofPlan, and verified-artifact records remain available through native
cellc and the VS Code workflow.
The browser compiler remains metadata-only and does not emit ELF. Omitting
native-only records and the optional browser semantic language service keeps
the default WASM bundle within its 600 KB gzip budget. The VS Code extension
retains full completion, hover, definition, and native-report workflows.
For CI And Local Development
Compiler caches and gate evidence now have bounded defaults:
incremental caches keep the 32 most recently used identities per root;
managed syntax, strict-backend, and CKB-acceptance streams keep three runs
per mode;
successful syntax audits discard reproducible per-case intermediates;
production acceptance removes its transient Cargo target and stopped-node
database while retaining identifying reports and verified artifacts;
identical large files are hardlinked only after their SHA-256 identities
match;
latest-<mode>.json records the exact report path, hash, size, and status;
cellc clean --cache also finds nested workspace cache roots.
Cleanup is confined to managed workspace and evidence roots. Symlinked managed
path components and non-regular cache payloads are rejected, cache entries are
created fresh rather than overwritten, and recency updates use create-new plus
rename. Operators can still override the retention bound for an external
archiver or an explicit debugging session.
Try CellScript 0.25
Install the exact release:
curl -fsSL \
https://github.com/CellScript-Labs/CellScript/releases/download/v0.25.0/install.sh | sh
cellc --version
For an existing package, start with the new review surfaces:
cellc explain generics path/to/package
cellc interface path/to/package --output target/package.interface.json
cellc check --target-profile ckb --all-targets --production
cellc build --target riscv64-elf --target-profile ckb --production
cellc verify-artifact build/main.elf --verify-sources --production
When preparing an upgrade, save the old and new interfaces and run
cellc interface-diff before publishing.

One note on the 0.25 language work:
the design and public interface for value generics are not final yet.

One note on the 0.25 language work:

the design and public interface for value generics are not final yet.

i am currently considering two bounded options—simplifying the public generic surface, or keeping user-defined generics package-local for the 0.25 stable line.

suggestions and concrete use cases are very welcome: [Language design] Choose a stable surface for value generics and public API signatures · Issue #23 · CellScript-Labs/CellScript · GitHub

recent_posts.content_text:
Thank you to the committee for approving the grant.
One thing before starting: the reduced funding of $700 (down from the original $1,600 request) lands at the same time the valuable feedback from Tianji surfaced a real gap in the design. The commit-bound two-phase construction needed to make the owner-freeze invariant actually hold (for both heartbeat/policy-update and ordinary spending) roughly doubles the state machine and test surface versus what I originally scoped, so at $700 I’d like to rescope the deliverable to match.
Proposed revised scope for $700:
Lock script implementing the corrected owner-op path only: BEGIN_OWNER_OP → PENDING_OWNER_OP → NORMALIZE / RECOVER, covering heartbeat and recipient-update with the commit-bound (CKB_SOURCE_INPUT header) time check from the review
Full adversarial and epoch-boundary test suite against that lock script (the pre-signed-and-withheld attack, late-normalize cases, replay protection, etc.)
Minimal testnet deployment exercising create → heartbeat → recipient-update → expiry → recovery for this path, so the fix is independently verifiable on-chain, not just on paper
Ordinary spending stays a single-step owner operation as proposed, outside this scope I’ll document that as a known limitation
Everything in it will be complete and independently verifiable rather than partial. Please let me know if this scope works. If you’d prefer something different, let me know.
Thank you.
